name: Cordero di Montezemolo Barolo Enrico VI 2010
text:
## Cordero di Montezemolo Barolo Enrico VI 2010

**The story.** Cordero di Montezemolo is a family estate in the [Langhe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langhe) hills around [Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alba,_Piedmont), farming more than 50 hectares, all certified [organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_farming). Its historic home is the Monfalletto site in the Annunziata hamlet of [La Morra](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Cordero+di+Montezemolo,+Monfalletto,+La+Morra,+Italy&t=k), and unlike most Barolo producers, who work many tiny scattered plots, its vineyards are large and grouped in a few sites ([Cordero di Montezemolo](https://www.corderodimontezemolo.com/en/estate/)). It also grows Dolcetto, Barbera, Arneis and Chardonnay.

**The wine: Enrico VI.** The name has a lovely double meaning. In 1965 Paolo Cordero di Montezemolo bought a prestigious Barolo vineyard; in 1959 his sixth child, Enrico, had been born. In the early 1970s he named the wine "Enrico VI" to celebrate both. The vineyard, about two hectares at 300 metres, lies in [Castiglione Falletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castiglione_Falletto), facing south-west, on iron-rich, compact clay, with vines over 50 years old. It is the estate's only Barolo from outside La Morra: a cooler, less ventilated site that gives what the family calls a "masculine" Barolo, sturdy and earthy, with prominent menthol notes, yet breadth and "an abundance of soft and sweet tannins" ([Cordero di Montezemolo](https://www.corderodimontezemolo.com/en/wines/barolo-enrico-vi/)). A UK merchant's sheet describes four to five days of maceration and ten to twelve of fermentation in steel, [malolactic fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malolactic_fermentation) in small French oak barrels, 18 to 20 months in oak and a further year in bottle ([Eurowines](https://www.eurowines.co.uk/download-wine-details/double-magnum-barolo-docg-enrico-vi-cordero-di-montezemolo)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [Piemonte vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/piemonte) calls 2010 "outstanding: a classic vintage with plenty of acidity, firm but ripe tannins and near-perfect balance in many wines". A wet spring caused irregular fruit set, but [Nebbiolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebbiolo)'s small, thick-skinned berries proved resilient; August was hot with cool nights, and early-September rain allowed slow, steady ripening.

**What the critics say for 2010.**
- **Falstaff: 96** (November 2014, [Falstaff](https://www.falstaff.com/en/wines/cordero-di-montezemolo-2010-enrico-vi-barolo-docg)). Bright, intense garnet; ripe wild raspberries and blackberries with a hint of cardamom and cloves; juicy and round, opening into "finely meshed tannins in many layers", with salty notes and a very long finish.
- **Eurowines** (merchant's note). Fresh red plums and cherries with lifted woody notes; layered, sturdy tannins that grip "gently and smoothly". "Lovely now, but better with time."
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.1** (from your CellarTracker list).
- (I couldn't read Wine Advocate, Vinous or Wine Spectator notes for this wine, so I've left them out.)

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is sixteen years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2018 to 2025, so by that measure it is at or just past its peak; from a classic vintage and a sturdy site, it is likely still in good shape, but drink it soon. Expect dried red fruit, menthol, spice and earth. Decant gently.

**Serving and food.** Serve at 16 to 18°C, decanted off its sediment. Classic matches: brasato al Barolo, roast veal, [tajarin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagliolini) with white truffle, or [Castelmagno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castelmagno_cheese).

**Value and where to buy.** BSW Liquor has the Enrico VI 2015 at $205 and the Monfalletto Barolo 2020 at $105, plus the Langhe Nebbiolo ($44.99), Arneis ($27) and a Barbera d'Alba; ZYN has the Langhe Nebbiolo ($40.20) and Arneis ($30.60).

**From the history books**
- **Barolo's villages.** Barolo is made in Barolo, Castiglione Falletto and Serralunga d'Alba and parts of eight other communes, including La Morra and Monforte d'Alba, south-west of Alba ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).
- **Hillsides only.** Barolo vineyards must be on hillsides; since 2010 the rules also exclude valley floors, flat and humid land and full north-facing slopes ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).

**Barolo through the ages**
- **Sweet before it was dry?** It was long believed Barolo was a sweet wine until the mid-19th century, because Nebbiolo ripens so late that cold cellars stopped the fermentation, and that [Count Cavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camillo_Benso,_Count_of_Cavour), mayor of [Grinzane Cavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grinzane_Cavour), brought in the Frenchman Louis Oudart to make it dry. Research by Kerin O'Keefe credits instead Paolo Francesco Staglieno, Cavour's oenologist at Grinzane from 1836 to 1841, whose "Staglieno method" fermented the wine dry ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).
- **"The wine of kings, the king of wines."** The new dry Barolo became a favourite of the nobility of [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin) and the ruling [House of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Savoy) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).
- **From merchants to growers.** By the mid-20th century large merchants dominated, blending grapes from across the zone; in the 1960s growers began bottling their own wines and single vineyards, and in 1980 Barolo became one of Italy's first DOCGs, with Barbaresco and Brunello ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).
- **The Barolo wars.** In the 1970s and 80s a group of producers, led by Ceretto, Paolo Cordero di Montezemolo, Elio Altare and Renato Ratti, began making more modern Barolo, with macerations of days rather than weeks and small new oak barrels, to tame Nebbiolo's harsh tannins. Traditionalists kept to long macerations and years in large casks ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).

**Curious details**
- **Named for a baby and a vineyard.** Enrico VI celebrates both the sixth child and the vineyard purchase in a single name ([Cordero di Montezemolo](https://www.corderodimontezemolo.com/en/wines/barolo-enrico-vi/)).
- **"Tar and roses."** The classic description of Barolo's aroma, and the wines turn rust-red as they age ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo)).
